newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan air dispute increases flight delays.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan air dispute increases flight delays.

text.p: Kenyan air traffic controllers in the fourth day of a go-slow on Tuesday increased pressure on the government to meet their demands by doubling delays on all flights out of the country.

An air traffic controller at Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport told Reuters that several hundred air traffic controllers since Tuesday morning had started to delay flights by two hours instead of one.

In addition to the delay caused at the main airport, delays from flights coming into Kenya to both Nairobi and Moi International Airport in Mombasa were already causing total delays of up to 12 hours.

"We are still continuing the go-slow and we have now started increasing the delay of the flights, departures are now being delayed for at least two hours out of here, instead of one hour," the air traffic controller said.
The Kenyan civil aviation authority said Monday evening that the government had started negotiations, but the air traffic controller said they had not yet received any offer worth considering.
"We don't have any confidence in what the government say. They have never been sincere and we don't think they ever will be sincere," the air traffic controller said.
He said that the group's initial demands for better pay and working conditions, including a 50-fold salary increase from $80 a month, was ready for negotiation.

"They (government) can come up with a figure and we will then negotiate from there, we are willing to accept less than the inital demands, but it's up to the government to come back with a serious offer first," he said.
Lufthansa Cargo and freight forwarders in Nairobi on Monday called for urgent action from the government to find a solution on the go-slow at the airport which are causing major delays to air cargo.

Lufthansa Cargo said the majority of all their Frankfurt-bound perishable cargo in the weekend had been more than 24 hours delayed because of the delays in Nairobi which have caused most of the distribution connections to be lost.

Airlink, an 85 percent-owned subsidiary of Swiss freight forwarders Kuehne & Nagel, said it stood to loose a cargo delivery of fresh cut flowers completely, which had awaited flight connection to Johannesburg since Saturday and still had not been send by Monday evening.

Lufthansa has a passenger flight, an Airbus10, with some 6.5 tonnes of cargo scheduled for Tuesday evening and a Boeing 747 freighter with a 100 tonnes plus cargo capacity scheduled for Wednesday morning.
The overwhelming majority, some 90 percent, of Kenya's air cargo is fresh produce -- cut flowers, fruits and vegetables.

All Kenya's airports have been crippled since midnight Friday, when air traffic controllers went on strike and started a go-slow, demanding better pay and working conditions. - Reuters Air Cargo Service Tel+ 44 171 542 7706 Fax +5017 - www.racs.com
